# Money movement and exit — non-resident taxation

Three of nine countries have no sourced rental rate — Panama, Greece and France.

## Spain — the base matters more than the rate

Two different taxes, kept separate here because merging them is the standard
error.

**Rental income.** Agencia Tributaria [37] gives the rate split directly:

> "Residentes UE, Islandia y Noruega: 19%. Resto de contribuyentes: **24%**"

A US resident is a third-country resident and falls in "Resto de contribuyentes"
— **24%**. Corroborated by the Modelo 210 instructions [38].

The base is the decisive part [37]:

> "El rendimiento a declarar es el importe íntegro que se recibe del
> arrendatario, **sin deducir ningún gasto**."

Expense deduction is available only "cuando se trate de contribuyentes
residentes en otro Estado miembro de la Unión Europea y desde 1 de enero de
2015, también en Islandia y Noruega" [37]. So an EU owner pays 19% **on net**
while a US owner pays 24% **on gross**. Mortgage interest, management fees,
insurance, maintenance, IBI and depreciation are all non-deductible for the US
investor.

The practical effect dwarfs the five-point rate gap. On a property with a 30%
cost ratio, the EU owner's effective burden on gross rent is 19% × 0.70 ≈
**13.3%**, against the US owner's **24%** — an effective differential of about
**1.8×**, not 1.26×. Grouped income cannot be offset between properties [37].

**Capital gains on sale: 19%** [38], listed without an EU/non-EU distinction,
unlike the rental rate. Single-source; the dedicated AEAT gains subpage was not
fetched.

**Mechanics** [38]: Modelo 210, rental income filed in the first 20 calendar
days of April, July, October and January, with an annual grouping option from
2024; sale filed in a three-month window opening one month after the transfer. A
fiscal representative is mandatory only in the art. 10 cases, and where the
letting is a permanent establishment [37]. A Spanish NIF is optional on the form.
**Modelo 211 is the buyer-side withholding on purchase from a non-resident
seller** — the form is confirmed, the rate is not in any fetched source. Do not
confuse it with the 3% *Gravamen Especial*, which is an annual levy on
non-resident **entities** resident in non-cooperative jurisdictions.

Watch item: the AEAT procedure page flags Orden HAC/623/2026 changing Modelo 210
filing deadlines for rented-property income; the detail was not retrieved [38].

## Mexico — 25% of gross, with a US-specific escape hatch

SAT states it flatly [39]:

> "El impuesto se paga aplicando la tasa de **25% sobre el ingreso obtenido, sin
> deducción alguna**."

Withholding [39]: a Mexican-resident tenant withholds and remits. Where the payer
is **also** a foreign resident, the owner self-assesses and pays **within 15 days
of receiving the income**. Where rent flows through a fideicomiso, the trustee
bank issues the CFDI and withholds — directly relevant to a restricted-zone
purchase.

**The escape hatch is specific to US residents** [40]. SAT ficha 53, under RMF
rule 3.18.5, provides an annual notice for "Residentes en el extranjero que opten
por determinar el impuesto sobre la renta (ISR) sobre una base neta", available
to residents of the United States. It must be filed **in January and February
each year**, via Buzón Tributario, requires a valid contraseña and e.firma, and
must list each payer's RFC and the amounts paid. Miss the window and the year is
taxed on gross.

**The net-basis rate that then applies is not stated** on the fetched page. The
election can be described but not quantified from this run.

Currency caveat: the SAT rental page is stamped "Última modificación: 05 de abril
de 2017" and carries its own disclaimer that portal information creates no
rights [39].

## Costa Rica — the best-documented of the Latin American three

From the Hacienda presentation [14]:

- **Rental income: 15%** on a base of gross receipts less a **deemed 15% expense
  allowance** (Arts. 29, 31 ter). Effective burden **12.75% of gross**.
- **Capital gains: 15%**, with a one-time alternative of **2.25% of the sale
  price** for assets acquired before 1 July 2019 (Art. 31 ter).
- **Buyer withholding on sale by a non-domiciled owner: 2.5% of the sale
  price**, as a payment on account (Art. 28 ter).
- Where the rent payer is a withholding agent under art. 31 quáter, the
  withholding is a **single and definitive payment** and the payer is jointly
  liable.
- Forms **D-125** (rent) and **D-162** (gains); payment within the first 15
  natural days of the following month.

**Source-quality caveat:** this is a 2021 presentation deck, not a regulation.
The rates should be re-verified against current Ley 7092 text before being
relied on.

## Panama — the priority gap, still open

The DGI's income-tax overview [41] confirms rental income is Panamanian-source and lists what
is deductible against it under art. 21 of Decreto Ejecutivo 98 de 2010 —
property taxes, depreciation of improvements, maintenance and repairs,
**third-party management fees**, condominium common charges, insurance premiums
not borne by the tenant, bad debts over one year old, and interest on
acquisition or improvement loans.

**It states no rate applicable to an individual's rental income, resident or
non-resident.** The page's "Tarifa" link was not followed, and the Código Fiscal
was not retrieved. Forms exist for remittance withholding (05, 929), transfer
tax (106) and capital gains (107), but no rate attaches to any of them in the
fetched text.

One structural finding does land [42]: residential leases are **ITBMS-exempt
where the contract term exceeds six months**; below six months the letting is
treated as non-residential and is subject to the tax. That is a tax-driven
argument for long lets in Panama, independent of the unknown income rate.

**Do not publish a Panama rental rate.** It is not in this corpus.

## Hungary and Italy — real numbers, wrong scope

Both of these are rates that look usable and are not, because the sources
address the domestic or general case and never mention non-residents.

**Hungary** [43]: 15% personal income tax on rental income, paid as quarterly
advances by the 12th of the following month; the taxpayer chooses a **flat 10%
cost deduction** (tax on 90% of revenue) or itemised costs including
depreciation; a corporate or sole-trader tenant withholds, an individual tenant
does not; residential letting is VAT-exempt with a HUF 12m threshold; a tax
number is not needed in the base case. **The page never mentions non-residents.**

**Italy** [29]: cedolare secca at **21%** of the annual agreed rent, **10%** for
*canone concordato* contracts, substituting IRPEF, surtaxes, registration tax and
stamp duty. For short lets [28], 26% since 1 January 2024, reduced to 21% for one
taxpayer-designated property. **Neither page states whether a non-resident owner
may elect it** — eligibility is expressed as natural persons acting outside
business activity, on property situated in Italy.

A material trade-off worth recording [29]: electing cedolare secca **waives the
right to any rent uprating, including the ISTAT index**, for the contract's
duration. And the 10% rate for *canone concordato* means the Italian tax code
pays landlords to accept controlled rents.

Presenting either the Hungarian 15% or the Italian 21% as the rate a US investor
pays would be an unsupported inference. Both are reported here as the general
rule with the scope limit attached.

## Portugal — 25%, via a two-step chain

The Modelo 3 Anexo F instructions [44] say only that rental income is "tributados
às taxas previstas no artigo 72.º do Código do IRS" — the rate is cited, not
stated. The rate itself comes from the consolidated text of Lei 56/2023 [21],
which amends CIRS art. 72:

> "2 - Os rendimentos prediais decorrentes de arrendamento habitacional…
> são tributados à taxa autónoma de **25 %**."

A duration-keyed reduction ladder applies on top — see
[tenancy-law.md](tenancy-law.md) — cutting the rate by 10 points for leases of 5
to under 10 years, 15 points for 10 to under 20, and 20 points for 20 years or
more.

**Two caveats on this figure.** It comes from a non-official consolidator, the
official gazette copies having failed [11][21]. And it is the general residential
rate, not a non-resident-specific one — but the chain to a US owner is sound,
because aggregation is residents-only, which locks a non-resident into precisely
this art. 72 special rate [44].

Two further things the source establishes, both adverse to a US owner:

- **Aggregation is residents-only** — "podem os respetivos titulares **residentes
  em território português** optar pelo englobamento" — so a US owner is locked
  into the art. 72 special rate with no option to be taxed at general rates [44].
- **Non-residents need not file at all if fully withheld**: "Os cidadãos não
  residentes apenas têm de entregar a declaração se tiverem rendimentos em
  território português que não foram sujeitos a retenção na fonte" [44].

Filing runs 1 April to 30 June, with payment by 31 August [44]. A reduced-rate
ladder keyed to lease duration exists under CIRS art. 72 as amended — see
[tenancy-law.md](tenancy-law.md) — but the base rate it reduces was never
sourced.

## Greece and France — nothing

**Greece**: every AADE page, including the "taxation of income of residents
abroad" guide, returns HTTP 403 to this run's fetch service [64]. No rate, no
mechanics, no representative rule.

**France**: no French tax-authority source was fetched at all. The French files
in the corpus cover letting rules, agency fees, eviction statistics and price
indices. Nothing on the non-resident rental rate, the *prélèvements sociaux* on
rental income, the filing form, capital gains, or the *représentant fiscal
accrédité*.

## Gaps

- Rental rate: **Panama, Greece, France** — three of nine.
- Capital gains on sale: **seven of nine** (all but Spain and Costa Rica, and
  Spain's is single-source).
- Withholding rate on sale: **all nine**. Spain's Modelo 211 and Costa Rica's
  2.5% are the only withholding mechanisms identified, and only Costa Rica's
  carries a number.
- Fiscal representative requirement: established for Spain only, and there only
  by exception.
- Repatriation and currency controls: **nothing for any country**. The IMF
  AREAER, the authoritative register, refused this run's fetch service [65].
